sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs independently, and these lower the risk: being a woman takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 1% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 8%, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 27% at 118 to about 17% at 175 beats per minute.

sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 20% at 0 to about 96% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 83% and chest pain brought on by exercise to about 32%, and higher cholesterol (from about 12% at 193 mg/dL to about 40% at 308 mg/dL) and more ST depression on exercise (from about 16% at 0 mm to about 38% at 2.8 mm) raise it steadily.

Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG raise it to about 24%, and two rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 and 17): an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG raises it to about 25% and a downsloping ST segment to about 28%; the ST segment also acts through the chest pain and blood pressure parts below.

This part gives each chest pain type its own amount: compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 1%, non-anginal chest pain to about 2% and atypical angina to about 9%.
Inside it, one small part adds risk for the 42 of 242 training patients with atypical angina: through it, atypical angina raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 41%.

A second small part reads non-anginal chest pain and a downsloping ST segment: through it, non-anginal chest pain takes the predicted risk from about 20% to about 19%, and a downsloping segment to about 21% (the model has little data on this, n = 17).

This part gives each thallium result its own amount: a reversible defect raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 40%, and a fixed defect lowers it to about 6% (the model has little data on this, n = 15).
A thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 89% (the model has little data on this, n = 2); a small part inside passes that code on, taking the risk to about 76% through it alone.

This part reads resting blood pressure and the slope of the ST segment: through it, higher blood pressure raises a typical patient's predicted risk quickly at first, then levels off, from about 17% at 110 mm Hg to about 25% at 155 mm Hg, and an ST segment that does not slope up raises it from about 20% to about 28%.

Blood pressure counts more when the ST segment does not slope up: across the whole model it takes the risk from about 72% to about 88% then, against about 17% to about 25% with an upsloping segment, rising quickly at first, then levelling off.

Inside it, a gate acts on 154 of 242 training patients, 63 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 37% without it and about 24% with it, and through the gate higher blood pressure lowers the risk in an uneven way, from about 28% at 110 mm Hg to about 13% at 155 mm Hg.
This part makes the predicted risk highest at about 59 years, lower either side: for a typical patient it goes from about 16% at 42 to about 18% at 66 years.

For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 99% without this part to about 99% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 53 of these 89 patients had heart disease.

Through this part, age only lowers the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 59 years: for a typical such patient, going from 29 years to 68 years moves it from about 20% to about 14% (on the training data only).

summary.text: The model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient, it goes from about 20% at 0 vessels to about 96% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 83%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 20%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher serum cholesterol as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 12% at 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to about 40% at 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) (on the training data only).
